Regarding the various sounds within a distance of several *li* near and far, one cannot hear those from distant lands in all directions. As for the two types of persons:

such a person attains profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*), whereby they can hear all sounds throughout a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*), and even all sounds throughout a medium two-thousand-world system and a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). They likewise hear them.
Regarding all sounds throughout the ten directions: if there is a person in meditative concentration who is silent and yet cannot hear any sound, there are likewise two kinds of such persons.
One kind of person has not yet attained meditative concentration; prior to the first dhyāna, they have attained the "subtle abiding mind," which is called "abiding in contact.
They are unaware of it themselves, like a person who is fast asleep and dreaming no dreams. This is Māra.

The *pishāca* seizes their consciousness; its appearance resembles meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet they have no self-awareness at all. They do not perceive it upon entering, but only when emerging do they realize their consciousness has been taken.
When asked where it went, there is another type of person who enters meditative concentration and hears no sounds whatsoever.

This person’s meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is slight while their offenses are heavy; they enter the "death-mind" absorption (*citta-nirodha-samādhi*). This is not wholesome meditation; it is an absorption that obstructs the Path.

Such a person is dull-witted and deluded, claiming, "I have now attained the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*. They also call this the "absorption of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*). This is not the path to *nirvāṇa*.
Even if one were to remain in this meditation for an eon, one would not exhaust the dharmas of the Path; it is called the offense of obstructing the Path.
It is also called "demons and spirits seizing one's consciousness," for the power of Māra sustains them in a state that resembles meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, there is another kind of person who remains silent in meditative concentration and hears no sounds from any of the various paths; this person is said to possess "sovereign meditative concentration.
If they wish to hear all sounds throughout the ten directions, they can hear them immediately; yet if their mind does not wish to hear, they do not.

One is able to hear it; therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Sovereign Meditative Concentration (*vaśitā-dhyāna-samādhi*). It is also named the Sun-Setting Samādhi (*sūryāsta-gamana-samādhi*). Why is this?
Formerly, while the Buddha was practicing meditative concentration in a forest hermitage within a field, there were two plowmen working nearby in the fields.
At that time, amidst the four seasons, there arose celestial winds, rain, thunder, and earthquakes; four oxen and two men [were struck] all at once.

He was terrified of death. The Buddha did not hear him. The man asked again, "The Buddha replied, 'I do not hear sounds. The man asked further, 'The Buddha has entered the concentration of no-mind (*acittaka-samādhi*).
The Buddha replied, "I have not entered the concentration of no-mind. The man asked once more, "If you possess mind and consciousness, why do you not hear?
The Buddha answered the man, "I possess mind and consciousness, yet I am always free from deluded thoughts. At that time, I intentionally enter [this state] three times a day."
It is obscure; because it does not grasp at sounds, it is therefore not heard. It is like the sun setting, when nothing is illuminated. I am also like this;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s sovereign meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Furthermore, it is like the case of Śāriputra’s meditative concentration in the mountains.
When he encountered a piśāca demon leading a host of demons as they roamed through the mountains, Śāriputra blocked their path and sat there to obstruct them.
He was not permitted to pass. The piśāca spirit became greatly enraged and struck Śāriputra’s head with a vajra as hard as he could, causing the trichiliocosm to tremble.
At that time, Śāriputra neither perceived nor was aware of it.
When he emerged from his meditative concentration, he noticed that his scalp felt somewhat unusual. He rose and asked the Buddha, "World-Honored One, my scalp now—"
"This was somewhat extraordinary. The Buddha said, "The piśāca demon struck your head with a vajra with all his might, causing the trichiliocosm to tremble.
This occurred because you had entered meditative absorption; had you not been in absorption, it would have shattered you into atoms.
He asked, "By what power of meditative concentration did Śāriputra enter such a state? The Buddha replied, "It was by the power of all meditative concentrations."
All are capable of this. If one enters the *vajra-prākāra-samādhi*, neither celestial Māras, followers of external paths, nor *piśāca* spirits can approach them.
Should they attempt to approach, the celestial Māras, followers of external paths, ghosts, and spirits will immediately shatter and perish of their own accord;

how much less could they possibly strike them? Question: All meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) are devoid of the mind of sensation and mindfulness (*vedanā-smṛti-citta*). How then did Śāriputra enter the great dhyāna?

Regarding concentration (*samādhi*): it differs slightly from the *piśāca* [section] on the head. He replied: "This question was asked so that future generations might know the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi-bala*).
By leaving this name for posterity, he guides sentient beings; this is called the Bodhisattva’s sovereign concentration (*vaśitā-samādhi*).

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possesses sovereign concentration such that whether entering or emerging from concentration, his body and mind remain in a state of meditative composure throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down."
It is neither fixed nor distracted; it can constantly manifest all Buddha-activities. A superior person can perceive that an inferior person is not so capable.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s sovereign meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Question: The six consciousnesses of sentient beings are the consciousnesses of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
they are not wisdom (*jñāna*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Rely on wisdom, do not rely on consciousness. Now, what kind of consciousness is this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)? And...
[Question: "If one can thus employ wisdom in various skillful ways without error, [how so? [Answer: "The employment of wisdom by all sentient beings differs and cannot be made uniform.
Foolish ordinary people employ the six consciousnesses of the sensory faculties (*ṣaḍvijñāna*). A bodhisattva at the initial stage employs two kinds of consciousness:

first, the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which is called awakening-wisdom (*bodhi-prajñā*); it awakens to and understands all phenomena, and its wisdom-understanding is unimpeded. Second is called..."
It is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), profound and unchanging. In the Western lands it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*;

in this land it is named Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), also termed the "Self-Nature Pure Store" (*svabhāva-viśuddha-garbha*), and also termed the "Tathāgata-garbha. If categorized according to its specific functions, it is named the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*).
When all phenomena are fully realized, it is called the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and mind (*citta*) have two distinct functions.
The six consciousnesses of ordinary beings are called "dispersed consciousness" (*vibhakta-vijñāna*), as they follow karma to receive retribution across the various realms of gods and humans.
When transformed by a Bodhisattva, it is named the seventh consciousness; it can overturn all evil karma of birth and death, which is itself nirvana, and is able to awaken ordinary beings.
The sixth consciousness, which divides [objects] into six parts so that they do not undergo transformation, is the *ālayavijñāna*. This seventh consciousness is named Vajra Wisdom (*vajrajñāna*);
it is able to shatter all ignorance, afflictions, birth-and-death, and fetters. It is itself the Buddha-dharma.
Just as a valiant general subdues the barbarian tribes and enemy thieves of the four quarters, such that all nations submit and become his subjects, so too is the valiant seventh consciousness.
The courageous vajra that decisively cuts through all phenomena is likewise so. That which is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is the eighth consciousness;

from the limits of birth and death up to the path of Buddhahood, it has never undergone change, whether in ordinary beings or sages, in the ignorant or the wise. It is as tranquil as empty space, possessing neither defilement nor purity.
Birth and death and nirvana are neither one nor two; though designated by provisional names, they are ultimately ungraspable. [Thus it is with] the five faculties...
One cannot see it; there are no words that can make it empty. Why? Because there is no emptiness and no non-conceptualization, nor is there any non-action.
It is neither joined nor dispersed. Its characteristics and its dharmas are likewise non-existent.
To understand that good and evil are like flowers in the sky is to realize suchness. One who can comprehend this is a sage; one who does not is a base person.

Although phenomena are neither one nor two, the ignorant and the wise do not dwell together. Those who do not understand this have [defilements], while those who understand it are free from all remaining sleep.
Chapter Four: On Postures While Lying Down.
When resting in sleep during the dark night, may all beings cause their various activities to cease,
their minds pure and free from defilement;
amidst the four modes of deportment, may they find the greatest peace and joy in sleep— the sleep of the Bodhisattva’s nirvāṇa.
When newly initiated bodhisattvas lie down to rest, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are utterly still and silent. They should know that all dharmas possess the characteristic of lying down:
they are tranquil and unmoving. What is meant by "rest"? That which is not precarious is "rest. Now, what is this so-called "peaceful rest"? It is being unmoving and...
"Flow" (*srotas*) means "to settle. What dharma is unmoving? What dharma does not flow? It is said that when the eye encounters forms, craving arises;
one must then perform various karmic actions. Craving is the movement, and karmic action is the flow.

Receiving retribution according to karma within the six destinies of gods and humans—is this not indeed flowing? As the Buddha told Śāriputra in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*: "Because the eye sees forms..."
That which gives rise to craving is ignorance; that which creates karma for the sake of craving is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).

That which consists of focused and single-minded mindfulness is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). Because consciousness creates karma, it wanders through all realms of existence. One should contemplate this eye: where does consciousness reside?
What is the faculty? Who is it that can see forms? From what do forms arise? The seminal essence is not the eye;

for instance, a person born blind whose visual essence is unimpaired and whose faculty is not broken cannot see forms, just like a person with healthy eyes. Yet, when one who was born blind passes away, they are able to see.
However, this phenomenon of blindness has no place of initial arising, nor does it have a place of cessation. The phenomenon of blindness does not [arise] of itself.
The eye knows that it is blind and can obstruct visible forms, yet it does not form the thought, "I am unable to obstruct visible forms.
Visible forms do not know of themselves, "The blind eye has come to obstruct me," nor do they form the thought, "The blind one does not obstruct me. Each is unaware of the other.
The eye and visible forms are likewise. What is the eye? The clear [part] itself is not the eye; the pupil is also not the eye; visible forms are also not the eye;
the vitreous humor and the tears are also not the eye; the sclera is also not the eye.

If each of these individually were the eye, there would have to be many eyes. Since there are not many eyes, one should know that each individual part is not the eye. If they were to constitute it collectively...
To say there is "one eye" is incorrect, for there is no combination [of conditions]. The blind person and each of the various conditions are all empty;

they neither gather nor disperse, and each lacks arising or ceasing. This is also true for emptiness and light; they are ultimately empty and quiescent. When observing in this way, there is neither many nor one; thus, there is no eye, nor even a name.
It is neither interrupted nor permanent, and it is devoid of the aggregates (skandhas) and realms (dhātus). There is no greed.
There is neither craving nor ignorance; they are entirely without characteristics, like being asleep without dreaming, seeing nothing at all.
Both clarity and ignorance are unobtainable. It is likewise with volitional formations and consciousness. Furthermore, there are no aggregates, elements, or sense bases whatsoever.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "The forms one perceives are equal to those of the blind. All dharmas are thus.
In the end, it does not move. That which does not move is that which does not flow. It is like when a person is lying down: all activities cease and there is no thought or perception whatsoever.
All dharmas are likewise; this is called "peaceful sleep. Not moving is called "peace" (*an-ā*). Not manifesting is called "hidden" (*gupta*). Quiescent extinction is the eye.
The Bodhisattva awakens by himself and further uses this dharma to awaken sentient beings, increasing their life of wisdom. This is called...

The meaning of the eye: the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) is the gift of Dharma. When a bodhisattva lies down to sleep, because neither good nor evil within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) can be apprehended, he likewise benefits sentient beings through this Dharma;
this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā). When a bodhisattva lies down to sleep...
Because all aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) are unmoving, benefiting oneself and sentient beings—this is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

When the bodhisattva lies down to sleep, because all aggregates and elements are without arising, abiding, or ceasing, benefiting oneself and others—this is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
When the bodhisattva lies down to sleep, because all aggregates and elements are neither fixed nor distracted— [this is called the perfection of meditation].
To be able to benefit sentient beings is called the dhyāna-pāramitā of concentrated wisdom.

When a bodhisattva lies down to sleep, all aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) are like flowers in the sky, devoid of any determinate characteristics. They are able to benefit all sentient beings within the dharma-realm, leading them to ultimate liberation;
they all attain bodhi and fully realize the meaning of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Although the bodhisattva sleeps, their emanations are universal.

He manifests the immeasurable dharma-realm. In all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), sentient beings, according to their capacities, find peace and rest, collectively realizing *nirvāṇa* and bringing all myriad practices to rest, like a person falling asleep. This is called the Prajñāpāramitā within the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s sleep.
It is the same for the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; as with the three aforementioned modes of conduct, they do not [cease].
To explain this further in detail:

regarding the fifth chapter on the complete possession of all superior flavors within the deportment of eating, when a Bodhisattva receives food and drink, they should first offer a prayer of blessing. With palms joined, they should direct their mind toward all the ten directions.
To all ordinary beings and sages, he spoke these words:
"This food, with its color, fragrance, and flavor, is offered above to the Buddhas of the ten directions; in the middle, it is presented to all the worthy sages;
and below, it reaches the various classes of the six realms of existence. Bestowed equally without distinction of priority, may all who respond to this grace be fully satisfied."
May all donors attain the immeasurable pāramitās.
When receiving food, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain the food of dhyāna-joy, free from any perception of other flavors.
When receiving food, one should wish that all sentient beings...
Having attained the food of the joy of Dharma and the perception of the flavor of ambrosia, when eating and drinking,
one should wish that all beings eat the meal of Nirvana and reach the perception of the further shore.
When the meal has been finished, one should wish that all beings perfect the knowledge of all modes.
Awakening the perception of sentient beings, having finished washing the mouth and drinking,
one should wish that all beings’ wondrous enlightenment may abide eternally, serene, clear, and pure.
When a newly initiated bodhisattva receives food and drink, they should receive it with a single mind, free from distracting thoughts.
When mindfulness arises, the fragrance is like a breeze of sandalwood; in a single moment, it pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
Sentient beings and sages alike respond to its presence, each attaining the supreme flavor.
When ordinary people smell the fragrance, they give rise to the bodhicitta; when hungry ghosts smell the fragrance, [they likewise attain liberation].
At once they were fully satiated and cast off their bodies as hungry ghosts;
when animals smelled the fragrance, they immediately attained full satisfaction and cast off their forms as birds and beasts to resolve upon the Bodhicitta;
when those in hell smelled the fragrance, they cast off the sufferings of hell.
Having attained the bodies of gods and humans, one generates the bodhicitta.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s receiving of food and drink:
giving to all, wherein both the giver and the receiver, as well as form, fragrance, taste, and touch, are empty, without arising or ceasing.
This is called the gift of Dharma, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

When a newly initiated bodhisattva partakes of food that is beautiful in color, fragrant in scent, and delicious in flavor, it permeates all practitioners so that they all attain the joy of the Dharma and are freed from the five fears; this is the gift of fearlessness.

Regarding the *dānapāramitā*: when a newly initiated bodhisattva gives food and drink—whether it be of excellent color, fragrance, or flavor—they do not regard whether sentient beings observe the precepts or violate them;
they contemplate only the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without any thought of differentiation.
It can cause sentient beings to still their minds regarding both sin and merit;
this is called the ultimate liberation of pure precepts, the samādhi of equality, and the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
For a newly initiated bodhisattva, the food they have offered possesses color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor.
It can cause sentient beings, upon smelling the fragrance, to attain mental concentration;

they obtain the flavor of immovability and deeply penetrate the true mark (*dharmatā*). With minds free from self and purity, they become fully endowed with the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
When newly initiated bodhisattvas give food as an offering, [this occurs].
Contemplate this mind of giving: it is without arising, abiding, or ceasing;
the food and drink given, as well as the recipient, are without arising, abiding, or ceasing.
Detached from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, it enables sentient beings to be satiated by the fragrance alone, free from the three types of conceptual thought.
Attaining the dharma of non-abiding, And being without coming or going—
This is called being endowed with *vīrya* (diligence) Among all the *pāramitās*. When a newly initiated bodhisattva receives food and drink,
He contemplates the donor before him And the mind with which the food is given.
Without arising and without ceasing, neither internal nor external, nor yet in between;
neither fixed nor disturbed, ultimately quiescent. There is neither the notion of extinction nor the absence of extinction.
My mind in receiving this food is also like that of the donor.
Regarding the mind that eats the food, it is one and non-dual.
For all sentient beings who receive my gift, myself, the assembly, and the three factors of the gift—the food, the recipient, and the giver—are all empty.
This is equal to the single *dharmatā* of the previous donor.
There is no giver and no receiver; there is no perception of food or drink.

Yet they can cause the roots of goodness in sentient beings to increase. Although the bodhisattva’s body and mind are always in meditative concentration, they can manifest throughout the ten directions simultaneously, according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Manifesting immediately in response to conditions, and hearing the preaching of the Dharma, one attains the Way according to one's capacity.
Knowing that the nature of afflictions is itself bodhi—this is called the dhyāna-pāramitā of tranquil concentration.
When a newly initiated bodhisattva receives food and drink, [they should maintain this awareness].
Contemplating the aggregates, elements, and sense bases: who sees food? Who consumes this food?
The food itself does not know, "I am food," nor does it know, "I am not food.
It has no self and no what belongs to a self; thus, even the word "food" does not exist.
Whether a bodhisattva accepts me or does not accept me, when a newly initiated bodhisattva contemplates in this way, there is no acceptance whatsoever, nor is there non-acceptance.
Knowing the nature of food and drink, they never waver; thus they attain the wisdom of immovability.
Entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata, [one realizes that] the giver, the receiver, and even the one who sees the food are all of the same nature as the food;
they have never wavered. Having attained this immovable wisdom, one is also able to know all phenomena as they truly are. This is called "knowing according to reality."
The Tathāgata’s true wisdom—why is this so?
As it is said in the sūtra, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, asked Aṅgulimāla: "What is the single training?
Aṅgulimāla answered the Buddha: "That which is called the single training is named purity."
This is the precept of the Tathāgata; it is not the precept maintained by those of the two vehicles—the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—as stated in the verse.
Aṅgulimāla further replied to the Buddha: "I shall now distinguish between the intentions of the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna."
The lives of all sentient beings All depend upon food and drink for their sustenance.
This is the Śrāvaka vehicle, not the Mahāyāna. What is called the Mahāyāna? Though they eat, they remain ever firm.
How is this called "one"? It means that all sentient beings All possess the Tathāgatagarbha.
Ultimately and eternally abiding,
when the newly initiated bodhisattva contemplates in this way,
they thoroughly understand that ordinary beings and sages are fundamentally and ultimately equal and non-dual. They are also able to skillfully penetrate this truth.
The beginning and end of all sages and ordinary beings are ultimately the One Vehicle.
The characteristics of their differences are also like the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*).

Regarding the "Dharma-realm ocean" mentioned in the context of the sense-base of form: this Dharma-realm ocean is the Dharma-realm treasury of form; the Dharma-realm treasury of form is precisely the Dharma-realm ocean.

Consciousness enters the ocean of the dharma-realm. That which is "consciousness entering the ocean of the dharma-realm" is precisely the ocean of the dharma-realm of the consciousness-store (*ālayavijñāna*).

That which is "wisdom entering the ocean of the dharma-realm" is precisely the ocean of the dharma-realm of the wisdom-store (*jñānagarbha*). It may also be termed the ocean of the dharma-realm of the accumulation of form (*rūpa*).
The accumulation of consciousness is the ocean of the Dharma-realm; the accumulation of wisdom is the ocean of the Dharma-realm. Both Buddhas and ordinary beings possess these fully;
this is called the ultimate equality of the fundamental and the derivative. This treasury of the Dharmakāya can be known only by Buddhas and Buddhas.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it is generally described as difficult to perceive; in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is analyzed so as to be easily understood. This is what is meant by "the Bodhisattva receiving food and bestowing food."
Although its nature is empty and quiescent, it is fully endowed with the treasury of Middle Way wisdom; it is also called the treasury of form, mind, and supernormal powers.
This is termed Mahāyāna Mahāprajñāpāramitā. To receive food and to bestow food is to be fully endowed with this meaning:
in a single thought-moment and at a single instant, form, mind, and sound pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions, enabling each of the three vehicles [to attain their respective goals].
Having attained that Way, they have mastered great wisdom and reached the other shore, as described above. In the sixth chapter,
"Demeanor of Speech," within the section on the Demeanor of Speech,
they are fully endowed with all manner of sublime and skillful vocal tones, universally responding to the minds of sentient beings according to their capacities.
When a newly initiated bodhisattva wishes to speak, they should first give rise to a mind of compassion, filiality, and obedience, settling the mind in right mindfulness.
All sounds then pervade everywhere simultaneously; though heard differently by ordinary beings and sages throughout the ten directions, these sounds universally manifest as offerings.
To the sages, they are heard only as songs of praise and eulogy, while bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions join their voices in praising the Buddha.
The asuras played the lute and the gandharvas performed music; devas and nāgas rained down flowers.

With all manner of exquisite offerings and the four requisites fully provided, they made offerings to all Buddhas and great bodhisattvas, as well as to all the various sages, without distinction. Beings of the six realms among gods and humans heard three kinds of sounds:
first, the sound of soft and beautiful speech; second, the sound of harsh and urgent speech, which subdues the stubborn and arrogant.

Sentient beings. Third is variegated speech: it is a voice that adapts to the occasion for the sake of subduing others and lacks fixed form. A single word of a Bodhisattva can produce all manner of sounds;

it arises spontaneously at the appropriate time without prior deliberation, responding to the capacity of the listener in accordance with their disposition. Such is the power of his unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*).

When gods and humans hear it, they become free from desire and attain the Way; when those in the four miserable realms hear it, they are freed from suffering and obtain happiness, and they develop [aspiration for enlightenment].

Regarding the bodhicitta: when a newly initiated bodhisattva observes speech, a sound emerges. Yet, when one examines its source—the throat, tongue, and teeth—none of them possess the characteristic of sound.
Why is this? Because the conjunction [of these factors] cannot be found. The lips are not the sound.
The teeth are not sound; the throat and tongue are also not sound. The jawbones and the palate are likewise not sound.
One cannot find sound when seeking it within each individual condition. The throat, tongue, and teeth do not know one another.
Their nature is neither a combination nor a dissolution. Know that this sound is like an echo in space: it is neither annihilated nor permanent, and it is without arising or ceasing.
It has no characteristics whatsoever. Furthermore, one contemplates where this mind of thought resides and what its characteristics are like.
When observing in this way, one knows that this mind of thought is neither external nor in between; it is like empty space, entirely devoid of characteristics because nothing can be apprehended.
This absence of speech—the name for which is "speech"—is called the gate of liberation through non-action. Although there is no speaker, it is able to...
With a single word, one universally manifests all sounds; with a single word, at a single moment, one manifests immeasurable words. Why is this so?

It is because of the power of original vows and great compassion for the sake of sentient beings. A single word can manifest immeasurable sounds, yet the perceptions and hearings of sentient beings differ from one another;
liberation is likewise so. Such is the power of the force of vows and compassion. It is not...

Yet with a single word and at a single moment, they can manifest immeasurable sounds; their physical bodies appear universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and the forms and colors they manifest before the eyes of sentient beings differ according to those beings' faculties, so that all may realize the Way simultaneously through awakening. Why is this?

It is because bodhisattvas who are newly trained, by virtue of their original vows, do not spare their own bodies or lives to protect the Buddha’s true Dharma, and through the power of their great vigor...
The power of non-retrogression consists in contemplating the bodies of sentient beings; with great compassion, one desires to deliver them.
Whatever is spoken—whether harsh words, gentle speech, or words that are piercing and varied—all of it is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
As the Buddha, the Sage, has taught: whether harsh words or gentle speech, though the sounds understood by the multitude differ, they all converge upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Throughout all lands, when sentient beings slaughter one another, the Bodhisattva appears in the world to subdue them and bring about harmony and peace; at times he becomes a human king or a celestial king.

Sometimes acting as a great minister of state, or appearing as a fierce general, he uses skillful means to subdue evil people and causes enemies from the four quarters to be pacified; he makes the nation prosperous and the people secure.
Sometimes appearing to practice the ten wholesome deeds, he uses skillful means to transform sentient beings; sometimes acting as a lord of a city, he creates images and transcribes scriptures.
Opening the gates, they practice extensive giving; through skillful means, they transform sentient beings.
Some manifest as śramaṇas who uphold the precepts without sparing their own bodies, extensively expounding the teachings of the Three Vehicles to deliver sentient beings by skillful means.
Or they manifest as young children, beginning their studies and first generating the aspiration for enlightenment; or they manifest again as those practicing and studying.

Appearing as one decayed and aged beyond a hundred years, or manifesting in cities and towns, or appearing to enter deep mountains, or manifesting the practice of anger and delusion—through such skillful means he leads sentient beings. At times he manifests as the fourfold assembly;
at times he is called a śrāvaka; at times he is called a pratyekabuddha; and at times he is the Unsurpassed Honored One.
For all bodhisattvas who are newly trained, A single sound manifests as myriad voices; With a single color, they appear in infinite forms through skillful means for the sake of sentient beings.
Through the power of patience and compassion, And the power of vows, meditative concentration, and supernormal faculties, They universally manifest in all manner of forms.

Because a newly initiated bodhisattva possesses the power of great compassion and the force of their vows, and because they skillfully exercise kindness and pity toward all sentient beings, whatever they say causes those who hear it to attain right faith and resolve to awaken the bodhicitta. This is called the perfection of the giving of Dharma (*dharma-dāna-pāramitā*).
Because a newly initiated bodhisattva possesses the power of the samādhi that accords with their own intention, at all times when they speak, they are able to...

May all sentient beings who hear this awaken and deeply penetrate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), transcending both the mind of emptiness and the provisional, and being free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

Seeing that all sentient beings—whether they uphold the precepts or violate them—are by nature neither defiled nor pure, and possess no marks of either sin or merit, they shall yet be able to uphold the precepts without sparing their own bodies or lives.
Through the power of their vows and merits, these newly initiated bodhisattvas shall thus benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

This is called the *śīla-pāramitā* of maintaining the precepts. When a newly initiated bodhisattva wishes to preach the Dharma, by means of this samādhi of the namelessness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), sentient beings who hear it find that the conceptualizations of their minds are stilled and they attain the *akṣobhya-samādhi*.
This is called the *kṣānti-pāramitā* of patience. When a newly initiated bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, whether the speech be harsh or gentle, its nature is...
It is equanimous and without arising, abiding, or ceasing. Sentient beings who hear it attain the Samādhi of Non-abiding. This is called the Perfection of Vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).

When a newly initiated bodhisattva speaks the Dharma, although a single utterance manifests as immeasurable sounds, their mind remains neither fixed nor distracted, enabling sentient beings who hear it to achieve understanding and realization, to resolve upon Bodhicitta, and to attain immovability.

This samādhi is called the dhyāna-pāramitā of tranquil concentration. When a newly initiated bodhisattva speaks the Dharma, sentient beings who hear it become detached from the aggregates and sense bases.
They are endowed with eloquence and immeasurable wisdom; [they perceive all things] as being like the body, like a shadow, like a dream, like a transformation, like a cloud, and like an illusion.
Because there is nothing to be grasped, they attain the Ratnaketu Samādhi, whereby they are immediately able to fulfill everything.

Samādhi. Attaining the dharanī-door of eloquence and penetrating the further shore of all ordinary beings and sages—this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of great prajñāpāramitā through the fullness of vocal deportment.
One fascicle of the *Dàsuí zìyì sānmèi* (Samādhi of Greatly Following One’s Own Intent). (End.)
